the present results do not exclude the possibility that the wearing of PMMA lenses may protect the eye from cataract formation, but the present results also do not support this thesis.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ocular lens autoflourescence increases with age, and that this increase is independent of the intensity of UV‐A reaching the lens.
PMMA contact lens wear does not protect the ocular crystalline lens against the development of cataract.
the UV‐A protection of PMMA contact lens wear is insufficient to prevent an age‐dependent lens autofluorescense increase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lens autofluoresence is not a useful indicator for the development of nuclear cataract.
the autofluoresence of the lens is an indicator of the lens’ age, but not of its health.
the ocular lens autoflurescence is a sensitive indicator of cataract formation and that the autoflurescence of the human lens can be used as a non‐invasive method for the study of cataractogenesis.
